findings.title: Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps full ID batches on every cleanup cycle
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) (and the analogous 'cleaned annotations by time/by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) unconditionally, even when the operation succeeded and even when len(ids) == 0. These are clearly leftover debug statements: the 'err' field is logged after it was already checked to be nil, and the level is Error for routine successful work. Combined with the cleanup interval being reduced to every minute (see cleanup.go change), every Grafana instance will now emit error-level log lines for all three annotation types plus orphaned tags on every cycle, including the entire batch of IDs (up to annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size, e.g. 32767 values per line). This pollutes error logs, defeats log-based alerting on errors, and can produce enormous log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug level without the raw ID slice.

findings.title: Undocumented 10x increase of the global cleanup job frequency
findings.body: The ticker in CleanUpService.Run was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description, which only describes the annotation-deadlock fix, and it affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotations: expired snapshot deletion, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, stale short URL deletion, and the query_history row-limit enforcement (which performs counts and deletes across large tables). Since a clean() run is allowed up to 9 minutes and a pending tick is buffered by the ticker, a deployment whose cleanup cycle takes a minute or more will effectively run cleanup continuously, multiplying database load. If the intent was only to make the (now smaller-batched) annotation cleanup run more often, the frequency change should be scoped to that job or at minimum documented and justified in the PR.

findings.title: deleteByIDs exceeds MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes
findings.body: deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID and only special-cases SQLite (999-parameter limit) by inlining the IDs into the SQL string. MySQL has a hard limit of 65,535 placeholders per prepared statement (PostgreSQL's protocol limit is also 65,535). annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size is user-configurable, so any configuration above 65,535 on MySQL or PostgreSQL will now make every cleanup batch fail with a parameter-count error, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE (which used no placeholders) worked at any batch size. The workaround should either inline values or chunk the DELETE when len(ids) approaches the dialect's placeholder limit, not just for SQLite.
